children: outlined an 18-year underground mine at its Pitarrilla project in Durango, Mexico, with estimated initial construction costs of $585 million and potential production starting in 2030, subject to permitting and a construction decision.

The feasibility study projects average annual production of 5.4 million ounces of silver, along with approximately 13,000 tons of lead and 29,000 tons of zinc. The mine would process 4,000 tons of ore per day and produce separate silver-bearing lead and zinc concentrates.

Chief Executive Officer Dan Dickson said the company is awaiting approval for a tailings storage facility, which he expects sometime in 2027. The study assumes a three-year construction period. If the permit arrives in 2027, Pitarrilla could begin production in 2030, he said.

Using a base-case silver price of $50 per ounce, the study estimates an after-tax net present value of $736 million at a 5% discount rate and an after-tax internal rate of return of 16.4%. Lead and zinc prices in the base case are approximately $2,028 and $2,734 per ton, respectively.
Over the proposed mine life, the study forecasts approximately $2.4 billion in operating cash flow and $1.7 billion in free cash flow. Silver would account for about 73% of revenue, Dickson said.

The initial capital estimate includes $65 million in contingency, with another $119 million in sustaining capital projected over the mine's life. Life-of-mine operating costs are estimated at $109 per ton of ore processed. After lead and zinc byproduct credits, cash costs are estimated at $12.66 per payable ounce of silver and mine-site all-in sustaining costs at $15.06 per ounce.

Dickson said the project's after-tax net present value rises by roughly $157 million for every $5-per-ounce increase in the silver price. At $65 silver, the study estimates a value of about $1.2 billion and an internal rate of return above 22%. At $30 silver, those figures fall to approximately $109 million and 7%, respectively.

Several approvals are already in place, including those related to the processing plant, underground development, explosives, water use and discharge, and land-use changes, Dickson said. The tailings facility remains the principal outstanding approval, along with amendments and extensions needed for the final design.

While awaiting the permit, Endeavour is advancing engineering, underground development and preparations for a construction camp. It is also working with Mexico's Federal Electricity Commission on power-line upgrades and substation engineering. Power infrastructure accounts for $77 million of the initial capital estimate.

Dickson said the company expects to fund most construction using existing cash and cash flow from operating mines. Endeavour expects to provide more detail on planned 2027 spending when it releases annual guidance in January 2027. It now expects to spend roughly $40 million on Pitarrilla in 2026, below an earlier budget of approximately $65 million, he said.

The feasibility plan covers only part of Pitarrilla's mineral resource. Dickson said future work could include drilling to upgrade inferred resources, evaluating lower cutoff grades if metal prices remain higher, and metallurgical testing of approximately 18.4 million tons of transition-zone material excluded from the current mine plan.

Management also sees longer-term potential for an open-pit operation targeting oxide material, although Dickson said the immediate focus is on building and operating the underground sulfide mine. He said the company's long-term vision includes evaluating whether Pitarrilla could support a 30- or 40-year underground operation; those extensions are not included in the feasibility study.

Endeavour Silver Corp. is a Canadian mining company that acquires, explores, develops and operates silver and gold properties. Founded in 2004, the company focuses on producing precious metals and expanding its portfolio through mine development and exploration. Its mining and development activities have centered on Mexico, including the Guanaceví and Bolañitos operations and the Terronera project. Endeavour has also expanded into Peru through its acquisition of the Kolpa mine, which produces silver as well as lead, zinc and copper.
